name: Magda "Screwhead" Szabo

inspiration.oldScript: Hellraiser dressed its demons in leather, chains and piercings, painting kink and leather subculture as literal hell and desire itself as damnation.
inspiration.newLens: Screwhead's horror is control imposed without asking, born of a daughter's grief for her father's store and a lifetime of having to be perfect to be allowed behind the counter. A chain someone chooses is never the villain here, and the Best ending turns on consent, boundaries and a little chaos she finally chooses for herself.

logline: She found the perfect fix for a world that keeps changing: tighten everything until nothing can move, and never ask anyone first. One quarter-turn at a time, Crystal Street is falling into perfect order.
backstory: Laszlo Szabo fled Budapest in 1956 with a toolbox, eleven words of English and a six-year-old daughter named Magda, and by 1960 he had opened a hardware store on Main Street. He painted the sign SZABO & SON because that was what a hardware store was supposed to be called, even though his only child had already sorted every screw in the place. In 1964, the day Magda cut her first perfect key, he climbed a ladder and painted DAUGHTER over SON, and left a little of the old word showing because he liked it when people asked. He sold nails one at a time, fixed anybody's toaster for a quarter and kept a green credit ledger for every family the bank turned away. Magda kept the books from age twelve. She also learned that a woman behind a hardware counter gets asked "Is your father here?" twenty times a day, and that the only answer is to be exactly right, every time, forever. In 1984 Starlight Mall opened a HomeMax the size of an airplane hangar, and by spring Main Street was boarded up. Laszlo died that summer in the dark, empty store, sorting screws into baby-food jars. Magda took a job at the HomeMax, where a manager half her age put her in Housewares "with the other gals" and rearranged the aisles every month. In October 1985 she bought a brass puzzle box from Oddment and Daughters because the shopkeeper said it "puts things right." She solved it in one night. Now she is Screwhead: gray-streaked hair scraped into a bun pinned with brass screws, a crown of screw heads glinting along her hairline, a tool belt hung with silver chains, and a growing Order of neighbors who smile, stand straight and never change their minds again. She never asks them. She is offering the whole street perfect order. Nothing will ever be lost, because nothing will ever move.

centralIssue.title: Control as grief
centralIssue.summary: Magda is not a monster. She is a daughter who spent her life proving she belonged behind her father's counter, then watched that whole world get bulldozed and decided nothing would ever change again. Tightening the street is how she holds on, and she has stopped asking anyone whether they want to be held. Help her grieve Laszlo, ask before you loosen anything, and remind her that a good fixer knows the difference between a bolt that needs tightening and a person who gets to say stop.

poster: A tall, gaunt woman in her late thirties in a brown shop coat with an orange hardware-store apron over it, gray-streaked dark hair scraped into a tight bun pinned with gleaming brass screws, a crown of brass screw heads along her hairline, silver chains spilling from her tool belt across a suburban street whose houses are snapping into a rigid grid, a glowing brass puzzle box floating in her palm
portrait: Close portrait of a sharp-eyed, grieving woman in her late thirties, gray-streaked dark hair in a severe bun studded with polished brass screws, a neat row of screw heads along her hairline, wire-rimmed reading glasses on a beaded chain, a name tag reading Magda, her face lit gold from below by an open puzzle box, chains glinting in the dark behind her
endingPhoto: A gaunt woman in a brown shop coat and orange hardware-store apron with brass screws pinned through her tight gray-streaked bun, calmly tightening a giant brass screw into a glowing puzzle box on a workbench, hanging chains and pegboard tools swinging around her in a midnight hardware aisle, teens frozen mid-step at the end of the aisle with flashlights
taunts: Lefty loosey, righty tighty. I only go one way now.
Is my father here? No. You'll have to deal with me.
Everything in its place. Everyone in their place. Forever.
My father sold this town one nail at a time. I'll fix it one screw at a time.
I don't ask. Asking is how things come loose.

clues.title: The Szabo & Daughter sign
clues.hint: Joey Benally says somebody comes to Rusty's every night to sort the scrap from a dead hardware store.

encounter.title: The Sorted Pile
encounter.text: Between a crushed hatchback and a tower of bald tires, someone has built something impossible. Every bolt, hinge, drawer pull and doorknob from a gutted store has been sorted by size into a hundred baby-food jars, lined up in rows so straight they hum. Propped against a dead refrigerator above them is a hand-painted sign: SZABO & DAUGHTER HARDWARE. KEYS CUT WHILE YOU WAIT. Under DAUGHTER, if you squint, an older word still shows through: SON.
encounter.art: A junkyard corner at dusk between a crushed hatchback and a tower of bald tires, a hundred small glass baby-food jars of bolts, hinges, drawer pulls and doorknobs lined up in perfectly straight rows on the dirt, a faded hand-painted wooden shop board propped against a dead refrigerator above them, a teenager crouching to look closer, orange sunset light from the left and long shadows, wide shot at ground level

choices.label: Ask Joey who has been building it

success.text: Joey rolls out from under a truck and wipes his hands. "Lady named Magda. Shows up at two in the morning, sorts till dawn, barely says a word. First night she told me my wrench grip was wrong. It was." Rusty bought the whole store's fixtures for scrap last year, and last week Joey caught her crying at the crusher, begging Rusty not to flatten the cash register. He shows you where it's hidden, under a tarp: brass, dented, still ringing.
success.alone: The junkyard office is empty, but the logbook on the counter is full of grease-pencil notes: Lady named Magda again. 2 a.m., sorted till dawn. Said my wrench grip was wrong. It was. The last entry: Caught her crying at the crusher, begging Rusty not to flatten the store's cash register. Hid it under the tarp. You lift the tarp: brass, dented, still ringing.
success.art: A teen mechanic lifting a tarp off an old brass cash register hidden in a junkyard, a hardware store sign behind him, a flashlight beam cutting through dusk

failure.text: Joey is elbow-deep in a transmission and tells you to come back when you can tell a socket from a spanner. As you walk away, every lid on every jar turns a quarter-turn at once with a single, perfect click.
failure.alone: The junkyard is deserted except for a radio playing to nobody, and the office door is locked. As you walk away, every lid on every jar turns a quarter-turn at once with a single, perfect click.
failure.art: Rows of glass jars in a dark junkyard, every lid twisting at once, a teenager freezing mid-step in the foreground

choices.label: Read the labels on every jar

success.text: Each jar is labeled twice: once in an old man's spidery Hungarian, and once below it in a woman's precise block capitals that copy the first exactly, down to his spelling mistakes. The last jar is labeled only in the old hand: APA'S LAST SORT, JUNE 1985. It is half full. Someone has never been able to bring herself to finish it.
success.art: A flashlight beam on a single half-full baby-food jar of screws, its label written in shaky old-fashioned handwriting, a row of identical jars stretching into the dark

failure.text: Your elbow knocks a jar off the row. The screws scatter across the dirt, then roll uphill, back into the jar, one by one, and the lid screws itself on. Somewhere deep in the car maze a chain begins to drag.
failure.art: Screws rolling uphill across junkyard dirt back into a toppled glass jar, a frightened teenager backing away, a chain trailing into a maze of stacked cars

choices.label: Take one screw out of its jar on purpose

success.text: You pocket a single wood screw. The whole shrine shudders, and for one second the junkyard fills with an old man's laugh and a voice with a thick accent: "Lefty loosey, Magdi! Not everything has to be tight! Not even you!" The sign is warm when you touch it, like it remembers a hand on a ladder, a brush, a fresh coat of paint.
success.art: A teenager holding up a single screw in a junkyard while a ghostly old shopkeeper in a brown coat laughs behind the rows of jars, faint and golden

failure.text: Your fingers lock around the jar. You cannot open your hand. You stand there until the sun goes down and a silver chain loops softly around your ankle, and only Barnaby's howl from the front gate breaks you free.
failure.art: A teenager frozen with a hand clamped around a glass jar at sunset, a thin silver chain curling around their ankle from the shadows

clues.title: The Szabos' credit book
clues.hint: Pearl Washington has lived on Crystal Street since 1959 and remembers every shopkeeper who treated her fairly.

encounter.title: The Credit Book
encounter.text: Pearl's rocking chair creaks while she cleans a rock-salt shotgun across her knees. When you say the name Szabo, she stops rocking. "Laszlo," she says. "Now there was a man who never once made me wait while he served somebody whiter first. And his girl Magda was the same, only faster." She has a cigar box inside she has never shown anyone.
encounter.art: A 71-year-old Black woman with silver cropped hair under a marigold headwrap and gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab army field jacket over a floral housedress, sits in a creaking rocking chair on her porch cleaning a broken-open double-barrel shotgun across her knees, a battered cigar box on the side table, a teenager sitting on the porch step looking up at her, autumn leaves on the lawn, warm late afternoon sun, medium shot

choices.label: Settle on the porch step and let her tell it her way

success.text: 1962: Harold out of work all winter, a bank manager who laughed at her. Laszlo opened a green ledger and wrote her name. "Pay when you can." The book has four hundred names in it, and from 1962 on, every entry is in Magda's tidy hand. On the night the store closed Laszlo crossed out every single debt in his own hand: FORGIVEN. "She kept that book better than any bank for twenty years," Pearl says. "Then she stood there and watched her daddy forgive the whole town in one night. And then the girl went and sat in the dark."
success.art: An open green credit ledger on a porch table, neat rows of names crossed out with the word forgiven in old ink, an elderly woman's finger resting on one name

failure.text: Pearl drifts into a different story, about a radio set in 1944 that picked up voices from a ship that had already sunk. It is a fantastic story. It is not this one. By the time it ends it's dusk, and across the street the Delgados are standing perfectly straight on their lawn, not blinking.
failure.art: Dusk on a cul-de-sac, a married couple standing rigid and unblinking on their front lawn, a teenager and an old woman on a porch across the street watching uneasily

choices.label: Offer to fix her sagging screen door while she talks

success.text: Pearl hands you a screwdriver from her kitchen drawer, its wooden handle worn smooth and stamped SZABO & DAUGHTER. While you work she brings out the cigar box: the green ledger, and a snapshot of Laszlo and a teenage Magda behind the counter, both laughing, the girl holding up the first key she ever cut, the new sign above them with the paint still wet.
success.art: A faded snapshot of a laughing old shopkeeper and a grinning teenage girl in braids behind a hardware counter, the girl holding up a freshly cut key, a freshly painted shop sign above them, a worn screwdriver beside the photo

failure.text: The screw strips and the whole door sags off its hinge. Pearl laughs until she wheezes. "Laszlo would've had that done in thirty seconds. Magda in twenty." Overnight, every screw in her door tightens itself so hard that by morning it won't open at all.
failure.art: A screen door hanging crooked from one hinge on a porch, an old woman laughing in her rocker, a teenager holding a stripped screw in dismay

clues.title: The letter under the level
clues.hint: Laszlo Szabo is buried at Pinecrest, and Father Iggy says his grave is the neatest thing he's ever seen, and not in a good way.

encounter.title: Plot 112, Perfectly Level
encounter.text: Every grave in Pinecrest leans a little, like old teeth. Except one. Laszlo Szabo's headstone is plumb to the degree, the grass around it trimmed with scissors, the gravel sorted by color. A brass level sits on top of the stone, its bubble dead center. Fresh chrysanthemums stand in a perfect grid. Nearby, Father Iggy pretends to tune his bass.
encounter.art: An autumn cemetery of old headstones all tilted at angles, except one gray headstone standing perfectly straight with gravel around it sorted into color bands, the grass trimmed short, a brass carpenter's level resting on top of the stone, chrysanthemums planted in a neat grid, a young priest with a black spiked pompadour, a white collar and a studded leather jacket tuning a red bass guitar on a nearby bench, a teenager kneeling at the grave, pale morning light, wide shot

choices.label: Ask Father Iggy about the woman who visits

success.text: "Magda," Iggy says. "Every dawn. Never prays. Just measures. At the funeral the undertaker asked if there was a son to help with the casket, and she lowered it herself, and wouldn't let it go until the straps were even. Took forty minutes." He digs out the program. Laszlo asked for his own words to be printed on the back: Things break. We fix what we can. The rest, we let go, and then we eat dinner.
success.art: A young priest in a clerical collar and a punk band T-shirt handing a folded funeral program to a teenager beside a perfectly level headstone

failure.text: Iggy is in the middle of a very serious funeral for somebody's hamster and shushes you. You wander off between the stones and find a fresh one, perfectly level, perfectly blank, with a brass level resting on top. It is exactly your height.
failure.art: A blank, freshly cut headstone standing perfectly straight among crooked old graves, a brass level on top, a teenager staring at it

choices.label: Lift the brass level off the headstone

success.text: Under the level is an envelope addressed MAGDI in an old man's hand, rain-stained, never opened. You read it, and it feels like opening somebody else's mail. "I am not sad, kislányom. A store is only a box. The town was the thing, and the town is still here. You never had to be perfect for me. You only had to be there, and you always were. Don't you dare spend your life keeping my shelves."
success.art: A weathered envelope addressed in shaky handwriting lying open on a headstone, a brass level set aside, a teenager reading a letter in morning mist

failure.text: The moment the level leaves the stone, every headstone in Pinecrest straightens at once with a grinding groan, a whole cemetery snapping to attention. The air smells like machine oil, and you run.
failure.art: An entire cemetery of headstones grinding upright at the same instant, dust and leaves flying, a teenager sprinting between the rows

signature.title: We Have Such Tidy Drawers to Show You
signature.text: The doorbell rings at 1:30 in the morning. On your porch stand Mr. and Mrs. Fenwick from down the street in matching pressed orange HomeMax aprons, smiling with every tooth, a thin silver chain looped politely around each of their wrists. Mrs. Fenwick holds a clipboard and Mr. Fenwick holds a label maker. "Good evening," they say together. "We're with the Order. We have such tidy drawers to show you." Behind them every mailbox on Crystal Street has been straightened, and the Lindgrens' garden gnomes stand in a perfect row, sorted by height.
signature.art: A smiling middle-aged couple stands on a suburban front porch at 1:30 in the morning in matching pressed orange hardware-store aprons, a thin silver chain looped around each of their wrists, the woman holding a clipboard, the man holding a handheld plastic tape-embossing gun, behind them a row of garden gnomes lined up by height on the lawn and every mailbox standing straight, a teenager in pajamas peering at them through a screen door, yellow porch light from above, medium shot from inside the doorway

choices.label: Say "No, thank you" and mean it

success.text: "No, thank you," you say, and you don't add a reason, because you don't need one. The Fenwicks' smiles flicker like a bad fluorescent tube; nobody in the Order has heard that sentence in a while. Mrs. Fenwick's pen hovers, then writes, slowly, DECLINED. They back off the porch, and for the first time tonight their chains hang a little loose.
success.art: A teenager standing firm in a doorway with one hand raised, a smiling couple in orange aprons stepping back off the porch with flickering expressions, their silver chains hanging loose, a porch light glowing

failure.text: "We heard you," says Mr. Fenwick, and he label-makes your front door anyway. It says OCCUPANT. In the morning there's another one stuck to your pillow.
failure.art: A neatly printed white strip stuck to a front door at night, a smiling man in an orange apron walking away down a perfectly straight garden path, a teenager staring through the screen door in dismay

choices.label: Invite them up for a tour of your gloriously messy room

success.text: You give them the full tour like a museum docent: the laundry mountain, the cassette avalanche, the band photos taped up at nine different angles. "And this sock," you announce grandly, "lost its partner in 1984 and has made peace with it." Mrs. Fenwick lets out a small, shocked laugh, then a bigger one, and her chain slips off her wrist onto the carpet. She sits on your bed and says she had a room exactly like this in 1962.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas giving a grand tour of a wildly cluttered bedroom with laundry piles and crooked band photos on the walls, a woman in an orange apron laughing on the bed, a silver chain lying on the carpet

failure.text: They follow you upstairs, and before you can stop them your room is perfect: hospital corners, cassettes alphabetized, every sock paired. You can't find anything for a week.
failure.art: A spotless bedroom with a tightly made bed and perfectly stacked cassettes, a couple in orange aprons nodding with satisfaction, a horrified teenager standing in the doorway

choices.label: Ask Mr. Fenwick what he loved before he joined

success.text: "Mr. Fenwick, didn't you used to fly kites in the cul-de-sac?" He blinks. "Kites," he says, as if the word is in another language. "Box kites. A dragon one. They go wherever the wind wants." One link of the silver chain at his wrist opens with a tiny click, and though Mrs. Fenwick hurries him away, he looks back at the sky twice.
success.art: A middle-aged man in an orange apron gazing up at the night sky with a faraway look on a suburban porch, one link of the silver chain at his wrist open, a teenager watching kindly

failure.text: He thinks for a long time. "Order," he says at last. "I have always loved order." He sounds like he's reading it off a cue card. The chain on his wrist cinches one link tighter, and somehow so does your collar.
failure.art: A smiling man in an orange apron with a blank expression on a dark porch, a silver chain tightening on his wrist, a teenager tugging nervously at a buttoned shirt collar

signature.title: Places, Please. Forever.
signature.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, midnight rehearsal
signature.text: You stop by the Glitter Box to help with the Halloween revue and walk into a nightmare of neatness. The Order got here first: every sequin is screwed down, every wig is pinned to a stand in alphabetical order, the spotlight is bolted to one spot, and Glory is frozen center stage mid-kick while Frankie's headset whispers, "Places. Places forever." At the bar, the Velvet Hammers, the leather-jacketed motorcycle club that always takes the back booth, are glaring at the brass chains someone has locked on over their own wallet chains. "Ours we picked," their president growls. "These, nobody asked." Out front, a line of regulars is gathering at the door, asking why the lights won't change.
signature.art: A small glittering drag theater at midnight, a tall drag queen in a magenta sequin gown and a platinum bouffant wig frozen center stage in a high kick, a single spotlight bolted in place on her, wigs pinned to stands in rows along the wings, a young stage manager in a headset standing stiff in the wings, three bikers in leather jackets at the bar glaring at brass chains locked over their wallet chains, a teenager in the aisle, hot pink stage light and blue house light, wide shot from the back of the house

choices.label: Jump on stage and improvise a number so wild nothing can stay in place

success.text: You grab a feather boa and launch into the most chaotic number the Glitter Box has ever seen: half disco, half Hokey Pokey, and a split you absolutely cannot do. Glory unfreezes at your first wrong step, shrieks with joy and joins in. Sequins pop loose like confetti and the spotlight wrenches free of its bolts to follow you. "THAT," Glory roars, "is a show!"
success.art: A teenager in a feather boa doing a wild chaotic dance on a drag theater stage, a drag queen in sequins breaking free mid-kick to join in, loose sequins flying like confetti, a spotlight swinging free

failure.text: You leap onstage and land exactly on your mark, perfectly, and then you can't move. You stand beside Glory, frozen mid-jazz-hands, until Frankie gets the work lights on at dawn.
failure.art: A teenager frozen with jazz hands beside a drag queen frozen mid-kick on a theater stage, harsh work lights at dawn, a stage manager in a headset rushing in

choices.label: Go performer to performer and ask what they want their act to be

success.text: You crouch beside each frozen performer and ask, "What do you want your number to be tonight? You can change your mind." A drag king wants to do Elvis instead of Sinatra; a queen in a ball gown wants sneakers. Every answer spins a screw loose. When you reach the Velvet Hammers, they ask you to take off the brass chains and leave their own, and you do exactly that. Their president nods. "You get it."
success.art: A teenager kneeling to talk with a drag performer at a theater dressing mirror, brass screws spinning loose from sequined costumes, a leather-jacketed biker at the bar nodding with her own wallet chain

failure.text: You ask, but the screws answer first: "Places." Every performer turns on their mark like clockwork, and the spotlight swings over and pins you to the stage. You stand under it, blinking, for a very long hour.
failure.art: A teenager pinned in a hard white spotlight on a drag theater stage, sequined performers standing stiffly on their marks around them, wigs in neat rows backstage

choices.label: Climb the fly rail and unbolt the spotlight

success.text: You climb to the fly rail with a flashlight in your teeth and find the spotlight bolted down with forty brass screws. Lefty loosey, forty times. When the last one drops, the light swings free across the stage like it's stretching, and wherever its beam lands, performers shake out their arms, gasp and start laughing.
success.art: A teenager perched high on a theater fly rail with a flashlight in their teeth unscrewing a spotlight, brass screws falling through the air, performers on stage below shaking loose in the swinging beam

failure.text: Screw thirty-nine strips. The spotlight swings up to the rail and holds you in its glare, and an intercom voice says, "Hold still. You're rattling." You climb down very, very carefully.
failure.art: A teenager clinging to a high theater catwalk in the glare of a bolted spotlight, a stripped brass screw in one hand, a dark auditorium below

signature.title: Main Street, 1960, Forever
signature.place: Main Street, Glimmer Falls, the night before Halloween
signature.text: Boarded-up Main Street isn't boarded up tonight. Overnight the Order has rebuilt it exactly as it was in 1960: the soda fountain, the barber pole, the five-and-dime, and in the middle of the block SZABO & DAUGHTER HARDWARE, its window glowing gold. Every shopkeeper is back behind every counter, smiling, chained to the register with a thin silver chain. Every clock on the street reads 5:59, one minute to closing, and the minute hands never move. From the hardware store comes the patient whine of a key-cutting wheel, and a calm voice says, "Nothing on this street will ever close again."
signature.art: A small-town main street at night rebuilt as a gleaming 1960 storefront row, a soda fountain, a striped barber pole, a five-and-dime and a hardware store window glowing gold in the middle of the block, smiling shopkeepers behind each counter with thin silver chains from their wrists to the cash registers, a round clock on every storefront with hands at one minute to six, a teenager standing in the empty street, warm shop-window light and cold blue night sky, wide shot down the sidewalk

choices.label: Wind every clock on Main Street forward to tomorrow

success.text: The bank clock, the barbershop clock, the big one over the five-and-dime: you climb, pry open each face and push the minute hand forward. 5:59 becomes 6:00. Closing time. All down Main Street, shopkeepers blink, untie their aprons and flip their shop doors to CLOSED, yawning like people at the end of a very long shift, and a few of them say goodnight to each other.
success.art: A teenager on a ladder pushing the minute hand of a big street clock forward to six, shopkeepers below untying aprons and yawning, storefront lights dimming one by one along a 1960 main street

failure.text: You push the minute hand forward and it snaps back to 5:59 with a click like a ratchet. Then every clock on Main Street turns its face toward you, very politely, and the shopkeepers ask if they can help you find anything.
failure.art: A teenager on a ladder at a big street clock frozen at one minute to six, smiling shopkeepers stepping out of glowing 1960 storefronts to stare up, thin silver chains glinting at their wrists

choices.label: Walk into Szabo & Daughter and look for the one thing she left crooked

success.text: Every drawer is marked, every screw sorted, every shelf dusted. Then you look up at the painted name over the counter: SZABO & DAUGHTER, and under DAUGHTER, faint, the ghost of the old word SON, left showing on purpose. From the back room comes Magda's voice. "He liked it when people asked. I tried to paint it over. It's the only thing in here I can't fix."
success.art: A teenager inside a spotless 1960 hardware store reaching up toward faded paint above the counter, rows of neatly sorted drawers, a key-cutting wheel throwing sparks in a back doorway

failure.text: Every drawer slides open at once, and every one is perfect, and you can't find the crooked thing anywhere. The shop bell rings. "We're closing," says Magda's voice. "We're always closing." Then you're out on the sidewalk with no memory of walking there.
failure.art: Hundreds of perfectly sorted hardware drawers sliding open at once in a gleaming 1960 shop, a teenager spinning in confusion, a brass shop bell swinging on the door

choices.label: Ride a shopping cart down Main Street and knock every display crooked

success.text: Dani pushes, you ride, and the cart screams down the sidewalk clipping every perfect display: a pyramid of soup cans, a tower of paint, a rack of postcards. Crooked, crooked, crooked. Behind you shopkeepers flinch, then giggle, and one starts restacking the soup cans into a smiley face as silver chains rattle loose all down the block.
success.alone: You get a running start, leap aboard, and the cart screams down the sidewalk clipping every perfect display: a pyramid of soup cans, a tower of paint, a rack of postcards. Crooked, crooked, crooked. Behind you shopkeepers flinch, then giggle, and one starts restacking the soup cans into a smiley face as silver chains rattle loose all down the block.
success.art: A teenager riding a speeding shopping cart down a 1960 main street sidewalk pushed by a laughing skate punk girl, soup can pyramids and paint towers toppling, shopkeepers giggling in doorways

failure.text: The cart hits a perfectly level curb and stops dead. You don't. You land in a pyramid of paint cans, and by the time you dig out, every can has been restacked around you, sorted by color.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled among tumbling paint cans outside a gleaming 1960 storefront, an overturned shopping cart at the curb, cans being restacked neatly around them in warm storefront glow

signature.title: Aisle Nine Goes On Forever
signature.place: A HomeMax that isn't there, 2 a.m.
signature.text: You walked out for a Bolt Cola and walked into a hardware store that should be the Quik-Stop. Orange aisles stretch to a vanishing point under humming fluorescent light. Every item is faced, priced and identical. A calm voice like a dentist's comes over the PA: "Attention shoppers. Please remain in your aisle. Order is being restored." Far down Aisle Nine, a tall woman with a crown of brass screws is restocking, and she does not look up.
signature.art: An orange big-box hardware store aisle stretching to a far vanishing point under humming fluorescent tubes, shelves of identical paint cans and boxes faced in perfect rows, a teenager in pajamas and sneakers holding a soda can and standing in the middle of the aisle, and far down the aisle a gaunt woman in an orange apron over a brown shop coat with brass screws pinned through her tight gray-streaked bun stocking a shelf, flat white light, long one-point view down the aisle

choices.label: Sprint for the exit sign before the aisles slide

success.text: You cut through Housewares, slide under a pallet as two aisles grind together like a sliding puzzle, and burst out of the automatic doors into the cold parking lot of the Quik-Stop. In your fist is a single brass screw, warm as a pulse.
success.art: A teenager diving through closing automatic doors into a night parking lot as the shelves behind them slide shut like puzzle tiles, a brass screw glinting in their hand

failure.text: The aisles close like a sliding puzzle. You turn a corner into Aisle Nine. Again. And again. You get out at dawn, but your pockets have been perfectly organized, coins by year, and you can't remember doing it.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager at the end of an identical hardware aisle with an aisle nine sign overhead, coins stacked neatly by year in their open palm

choices.label: Knock every can of paint off the shelves

success.text: Thirty colors explode across the spotless floor: tangerine, teal, a purple called Midnight Rendezvous. The PA screams static. Disorder tears through the store like wet paper and you wake up in the Quik-Stop lot, splattered teal, cackling.
success.art: Paint cans bursting across a perfect hardware store floor in splashes of tangerine, teal and purple, the shelves tearing apart like wet paper, a delighted teenager in the middle

failure.text: Every can you shove lands upright, label forward. A soft chain loops your ankle. "Thank you for shopping," says the PA. You come to in a parked car with your seatbelt fastened, very, very tight.
failure.art: Paint cans landing perfectly upright on a gleaming floor, labels facing forward, a silver chain curling around a sneaker

choices.label: Ask the clerk, politely, where they keep the tools for loosening

success.text: She stops. The screws in her crown catch the light. Nobody in this store has asked her a real question in a year. "We don't... stock those anymore," she says, and for one second she looks like a tired woman in an orange apron who hasn't slept since summer. She points you to the exit without a word.
success.art: A gaunt woman clerk in an orange apron with brass screws pinned through her bun pausing mid-restock, her face suddenly sad and human, pointing a teenager toward a glowing exit

failure.text: "Everything you need is in your aisle," she says, without turning around. Your jacket zipper zips itself to your chin, and your shoelaces knot themselves into perfect, impossible double bows.
failure.art: A teenager's jacket zipper sliding up by itself under fluorescent light, shoelaces tying themselves into bows, a woman clerk's back turned in the distance

signature.title: The Leveling
signature.text: You wake to a sound like a thousand ratchets. Out your window, Crystal Street is rearranging itself: the houses grinding on their foundations into a perfect grid, crooked mailboxes snapping plumb, the round Heartstone garden squaring off into a box. Neighbors stand at their mailboxes in pajamas with silver chains looped kindly around their wrists. Even Mr. and Mr. Abernathy-Cole, who mow in zigzags on principle, are standing at attention. "Nobody asked us," one of them says through a fixed smile, "but it's fine." "It doesn't hurt," calls Mrs. Delgado. "Nothing moves. Isn't it wonderful?"
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at midnight seen from a bedroom window, ranch houses grinding sideways on their foundations into a rigid square grid, crooked mailboxes snapping upright, neighbors in pajamas standing at their mailboxes with thin silver chains around their wrists and fixed calm smiles, two middle-aged men in matching robes standing at attention by a zigzag-mowed lawn, a round garden at the center with a purple crystal rock as its edges turn square, white streetlight, high wide shot

choices.label: Go house to house and ask each neighbor if they want out

success.text: You ask each of them out loud: "Do you want this off?" It takes a while for anyone to find the word, but for every neighbor who manages a yes, the chain goes slack with a little sigh. Mrs. Delgado blinks and asks why she's on the lawn in her curlers. The Abernathy-Coles immediately go back to bickering about the hedges, and three houses grind back to their crooked, perfect places.
success.art: A teenager twisting a silver chain loose from a woman's wrist at a mailbox, the chain falling slack, two men in bathrobes arguing happily behind them as houses settle back askew

failure.text: You loosen one link and it tightens on you instead. You spend the rest of the night chained gently to the Delgados' mailbox, watching the street square itself. The morning paper calls it a freak frost heave.
failure.art: A teenager chained by one wrist to a suburban mailbox at dawn, the street behind them laid out in an eerie perfect grid, a newspaper on the lawn

choices.label: Crank a boombox and get everyone dancing badly

success.text: You put on the loudest thing you own and do the worst Running Man in Glimmer Falls history. Nobody can stay level while they're laughing. The Abernathy-Coles start voguing. Mrs. Delgado does the Bump. Chains clatter off wrists onto the asphalt. Order cannot survive the Electric Slide.
success.art: Neighbors in pajamas dancing wildly on a cul-de-sac at midnight around a blaring boombox, silver chains dropping off their wrists, a teenager in glow bracelets leading the chaos

failure.text: They dance. All of them, in perfect unison, precise as a drill team, smiling the same smile. You are the only one off the beat, and on the next count every head on Crystal Street turns to look at you.
failure.art: Rows of neighbors in pajamas dancing in flawless unison on a gridded street, every head turned toward one teenager holding a boombox

signature.title: Some Assembly Required
signature.text: The flat-pack wardrobe your mom bought at HomeMax has been leaning in its box against your wall for a week. At 2 a.m. the box splits open by itself. Panels slide out, cam locks spin, dowels pop into holes, and an Allen key turns in midair with a patient click, click, click. The instruction booklet flutters open on your carpet to the last page. Step 47 is a neat little drawing of you, folded up and tucked into the bottom drawer, with a smiley face.
signature.art: A dark 1980s teenage bedroom at two in the morning, a flat-pack wardrobe assembling itself in midair beside the wall, pale wooden panels sliding into place, dowels and brass screws floating, an Allen key turning by itself, the torn cardboard box split open on the carpet with an instruction booklet open beside it, a wide-eyed teenager sitting up in bed clutching a blanket, cold moonlight through the window and a warm desk lamp glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Follow the instructions backward, step 47 to step 1

success.text: You grab the booklet and start at the end. Step 46: remove the drawer. Step 45: unscrew the hinges. Every step you undo, the wardrobe undoes too, until it lies in a flat, harmless stack on your carpet with a little bag of leftover screws on top. Somewhere very far away, a woman sighs like a store intercom: "Lefty loosey."
success.art: A teenager kneeling on a bedroom carpet holding an open instruction booklet, a wardrobe collapsing back into a neat stack of flat panels, a small plastic bag of brass screws resting on top

failure.text: You lose your place around step 30. The wardrobe doesn't. It finishes itself, opens its doors and gently scoops up your posters, your cassettes and your laundry and puts them all away, folded and sorted. You can't find anything for a week, and you're pretty sure that was the point.
failure.art: A perfectly assembled wardrobe with its doors open in a bedroom that has been stripped neat and bare, every cassette and sweater folded and sorted inside, a bewildered teenager holding a crumpled instruction booklet

choices.label: Steal one screw and hide it where it can never be found

success.text: Every flat-pack comes with one screw too few. You make sure of it. You snatch a brass screw out of the air and drop it down the heating vent. The wardrobe gets to the last step, wobbles, tries again, wobbles, and finally just leans against the wall, almost done and very confused, which is how every wardrobe in history has ended up.
success.art: A lopsided half-built wardrobe leaning against a bedroom wall, one door hanging crooked, a grinning teenager crouched by a floor vent dropping in a single brass screw

failure.text: The screw wriggles out of your fist like a minnow and darts back into its hole. A drawer slides open behind you, very politely, and waits. You spend the rest of the night sleeping in the bathtub with the door locked and a toilet plunger for company.
failure.art: A teenager curled up asleep in a bathtub clutching a toilet plunger, a bathroom door locked tight, a wardrobe drawer peeking open in the dark bedroom beyond

choices.label: Stand in front of it and tell it, clearly, that you did not agree to this

success.text: "Stop," you say. "I didn't ask for this. I don't want to be in a drawer." The Allen key freezes mid-turn. For a second nothing in the room moves at all, and then, very slowly, the key turns the other way. The panels sag. It's almost as if no one had ever said that to it before.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas standing firm with one hand raised before a half-assembled wardrobe, a hex key frozen in midair and beginning to turn backward, panels sagging apart

failure.text: Your voice cracks halfway through, and it comes out as a question. The wardrobe takes a question as a yes. You wake up in the morning in the bottom drawer, folded up comfortably, with a smiley-face sticky note on your knee that reads PERFECT.
failure.art: A teenager waking up folded snugly inside the bottom drawer of a wardrobe, knees tucked to chin, a yellow sticky note on one knee, morning light through the blinds

signature.title: Screwed Shut
signature.text: You wake to the whine of a power drill. Then another, and another, all around the house. Through the gap in your curtains you see neighbors in pajamas screwing plywood over your windows, a brass screw every four inches, perfectly spaced, and the same thing is happening to every house on Crystal Street. The front door is already sealed. Through the mail slot comes a calm voice like a store intercom: "Stay in. It's safer. Nothing that's fastened can ever be lost."
signature.art: A dark suburban hallway at three in the morning seen from inside the house, plywood boards screwed over every window from outside with brass screw tips poking through in an even grid, drill bits glinting through the wood, a front door with a brass mail slot glowing from a porch light outside, a teenager in pajamas kneeling at the mail slot in alarm, thin yellow light leaking through gaps in the boards, medium shot

choices.label: Talk through the mail slot and ask if they want to be doing this

success.text: You kneel by the mail slot. "Hey. Did anyone ask you if you wanted to do this?" The drilling stops. A long pause, and then a voice you know, Mr. Brubaker the mailman, quiet and confused: "No. She didn't ask. I was going to go fishing this weekend." You hear him set the drill down, and then, slowly, start backing the screws out.
success.art: A teenager kneeling and speaking through a brass mail slot in a front door at night, on the porch outside a confused mailman lowering a power drill, a silver chain slipping loose from his wrist

failure.text: The mail slot snaps shut on your fingers, not hard, just firmly, like a hand patting yours. "Don't fuss," says the voice. "You'll thank me." Then a single brass screw twists through the flap itself, sealing it, perfectly centered.
failure.art: A teenager shaking their stung fingers beside a front door as a single brass screw twists through the center of a brass mail slot, warm hallway light

choices.label: Unscrew the boards from the inside with a butter knife

success.text: You wedge a butter knife into the first screw head and turn. Lefty loosey. It fights you, then gives. Screw after screw drops into your palm, warm as pennies, until the board swings loose and cold night air pours in. Up and down the street, kids at their windows watch you, then reach for their own butter knives.
success.art: A teenager twisting a butter knife against brass screws on plywood over a bedroom window, loose screws piling in their palm, cold moonlight spilling through a widening gap

failure.text: Every screw you loosen tightens itself again with a sound like a ratchet, and the knife bends into a perfect right angle. By dawn your hands ache, the board is tighter than ever, and the butter knife has been put back in the silverware drawer, sorted by size.
failure.art: A tired teenager slumped against a plywood-covered window at dawn holding a butter knife bent into a perfect right angle, brass screws gleaming in tight rows

choices.label: Kick out the attic vent and climb onto the roof

success.text: You shove past boxes of Christmas lights, kick out the attic vent and crawl onto the shingles. From up here you can see the whole street: neighbors with drills, plywood going up, and on the roundabout a tall woman crowned with brass screws, conducting it all like an orchestra. You wave your arms and yell. Below, a few of the drillers stop and look up, uncertain.
success.art: A teenager standing on a moonlit suburban roof waving their arms, neighbors below holding power drills pausing to look up, a tall woman crowned with brass screws raising her hands on a distant roundabout

failure.text: The attic vent is screwed shut from outside too, and when you push on it, the whole attic tidies itself around you: boxes stacked, cords coiled, holiday decorations sorted by season. You spend the rest of the night wedged between Easter and the Fourth of July.
failure.art: A teenager wedged between neatly stacked storage boxes in a cramped attic, coiled extension cords and sorted holiday decorations all around, a sealed vent glinting with brass screws

signature.title: Clockwise Forever
signature.place: The roller-rink annex at Pump Iron, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The rink should be closed, but the mirror ball is turning and the organ is playing the same eight bars over and over. Out on the floor, fifty skaters glide in a perfect circle, clockwise, single file, each exactly one arm's length from the next, linked wrist to wrist by thin silver chains. Their faces are calm. Their ankles are wobbling. A freshly painted banner over the DJ booth, in neat capitals, reads: ALL SKATE. CLOCKWISE. FOREVER.
signature.art: A 1980s roller rink at eleven at night under a spinning mirror ball, fifty skaters gliding single file in a perfect clockwise circle, each linked wrist to wrist to the next by a thin silver chain, calm faces and wobbling ankles, a freshly painted cloth strip hanging over the DJ booth, an organ in the corner, a teenager standing at the rail in rental skates, scattered white sparkles from the mirror ball and magenta floor light, wide shot from the rail

choices.label: Lace up and skate the wrong way, as fast as you can

success.text: Sunny whoops and takes the lead, and you skate counterclockwise straight into the current, weaving between the chained skaters like salmon. Every time you pass someone, they wobble, glance back and grin. By your fifth lap half the rink has broken formation, and the organ hits a wrong note and keeps it.
success.alone: You whoop and push off, skating counterclockwise straight into the current, weaving between the chained skaters like a salmon. Every time you pass someone, they wobble, glance back and grin. By your fifth lap half the rink has broken formation, and the organ hits a wrong note and keeps it.
success.art: A grinning wheelchair racer and a teenager on roller skates speeding counterclockwise through a ring of chained skaters under a mirror ball, skaters breaking formation and laughing

failure.text: The circle pulls at you like a whirlpool. Your skates turn by themselves, and before you know it you're in the line, a chain looped kindly around your wrist, gliding clockwise to the same eight bars until your legs give out at dawn.
failure.art: An exhausted teenager on roller skates gliding in a perfect circle of skaters at dawn, a thin silver chain around their wrist, a mirror ball turning slowly overhead

choices.label: Take over the DJ booth and call a Hokey Pokey

success.text: Mix grabs the mic like he was born there. "Alright, Glimmer Falls, everybody stop where you are. Left foot in!" Fifty skaters, unable to resist a direct instruction, stop dead. Then they have to choose which way to turn themselves around, and every single one chooses differently. The chains tangle, snap and fall to the floor like tinsel.
success.alone: You grab the mic like you were born there. "Alright, Glimmer Falls, everybody stop where you are. Left foot in!" Fifty skaters, unable to resist a direct instruction, stop dead. Then they have to choose which way to turn themselves around, and every single one chooses differently. The chains tangle, snap and fall to the floor like tinsel.
success.art: A teen DJ in a booth speaking into a microphone with a grin, skaters on the rink floor doing a silly dance in every different direction, silver chains snapping and falling like tinsel

failure.text: "Left foot in," you announce, and the skaters do it, perfectly, in unison, and then keep doing it, exactly as instructed, because you never told them how the dance ends. You stay up all night calling verses.
failure.art: A tired teenager slumped over a DJ booth microphone while dozens of skaters on the rink below perform the same dance step in eerie perfect unison under a mirror ball

choices.label: Skate alongside each one and ask if they want to stop

success.text: You fall into step beside a girl from your algebra class and ask, "Do you want to keep going?" She blinks. "My feet hurt so bad," she whispers. "Nobody asked." You unhook her chain, and she sits down on the bench and laughs. You go down the line one skater at a time, and everyone who says stop gets to stop.
success.art: A teenager skating beside a tired girl in a ring of chained skaters, gently unhooking a silver chain from her wrist, others on a bench at the edge pulling off their skates and laughing

failure.text: You ask the first skater. She smiles and says, "I'm fine," in a voice like an intercom, and before you can ask the next one, the line has looped around you twice. Now you're skating clockwise too, asking "Do you want to stop?" to the back of somebody's head, lap after lap, all night.
failure.art: A teenager caught in a circle of skaters linked by silver chains, gliding clockwise under a mirror ball, calling out to the skater ahead with a worried face

signature.title: The Box Solves Itself
signature.text: The brass puzzle box is on your nightstand. You never brought it home. It's turning by itself, panels clicking and sliding, each click a little louder, and with every click your room gets neater: posters squared, sheets tucked hospital-tight, cassettes alphabetized. From a seam of gold light, chains begin to unspool across the walls, and a woman's voice like a store intercom says, "One more turn and you'll never lose anything again. You don't have to say yes. I've already decided."
signature.art: A cluttered 1980s teenage bedroom at 3:33 in the morning snapping into perfect order, cassettes stacking themselves in rows, bed sheets pulling tight, a brass puzzle box on the nightstand turning by itself with golden light pouring from a seam, thin silver chains unspooling out of the light across the walls and shelves, a teenager in pajamas sitting up in bed staring at it, gold light from the box and blue shadow, medium shot

choices.label: Grab the box and hold its panels still

success.text: The panels grind against your palms like a living thing. You hold on. The last panel strains, shudders, and stops a hair from closing. The chains retract with a sulky rattle, and your room explodes back into its glorious mess.
success.art: A teenager gripping a glowing brass puzzle box with both hands, knuckles white, chains snapping back into the walls, laundry and cassettes tumbling back into disorder

failure.text: The box completes its turn. You wake to a perfect room and one thin silver chain looped around your wrist, too tight to slip off and too loose to hurt. You find yourself making your bed without deciding to.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a perfectly made bed in an eerily tidy room, staring at a thin silver chain around their wrist, a closed brass box on the nightstand

choices.label: Solve the box backward, lefty loosey

success.text: You turn every panel the wrong way. The box unravels with a sound like a long-held breath let out. Inside there are no chains, only a small brass key tag stamped SZABO & DAUGHTER. KEYS CUT WHILE YOU WAIT. It feels like something somebody was meant to find.
success.art: An unfolded brass puzzle box lying open and harmless on a bedspread, a small brass key tag inside catching the lamplight, a teenager leaning over it in wonder

failure.text: The panels reverse under your fingers and solve themselves twice as fast. Your shoelaces tie into knots it will take a week to undo, and every drawer in your room locks with a satisfied click.
failure.art: A brass puzzle box spinning its panels in a blur under a teenager's frantic fingers, dresser drawers slamming shut around the room

choices.label: Open the window and hurl it as far as you can

success.text: It sails over the fence, over the Delgados' roof, and lands somewhere far off with a clang like a dropped toolbox. The chains snap back into the wall. It'll be back. But not tonight.
success.art: A teenager leaning out a bedroom window having just hurled a glowing brass box into the night sky over suburban rooftops, chains whipping back into the room

failure.text: You throw it hard. You hear it land. Then you hear it coming back, click by click, up the drainpipe, across the roof. When you turn around it is on your nightstand again, polished, warm and one turn closer.
failure.art: A brass puzzle box sitting back on a nightstand, gleaming, while a frightened teenager stands at an open window staring at it

finale.title: Closing Time at Szabo & Daughter
finale.text: On Halloween the Heartstone opens like a puzzle box and Crystal Street folds inside it. You stand in a perfect copy of Szabo & Daughter Hardware, every drawer labeled in her precise capitals, every neighbor standing in an aisle with a silver chain around their wrist, smiling. Behind the counter Magda works a key-cutting wheel that throws sparks like fireworks. She wears her HomeMax apron over her father's brown shop coat, the sleeves rolled twice. "Nothing will ever close again," she says. "Not on my watch. And nobody will ever walk in here again and ask me if my father is around."
finale.art: A vast hardware store inside a glowing purple crystal cavern, endless walls of little wooden drawers, smiling neighbors in pajamas standing in every aisle with thin silver chains around their wrists, behind a long counter a gaunt woman with brass screws pinned through her tight gray-streaked bun, wire-rimmed glasses on a beaded chain, an orange apron over a brown shop coat with rolled sleeves, works a key-cutting wheel that throws a shower of orange sparks, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes facing her across the counter, violet crystal light and orange sparks, wide shot

choices.label: Find the gap you found the first nights: the one screw her perfect store can't spare, and pull it

success.text: You learned it the first nights of the week, in Aisle Nine, at the foot of a flat-pack wardrobe, on your own front porch: every perfect order has a gap, one missing screw, one question it can't answer, one plain no. So while Magda watches the crew, you walk the aisles looking for hers, and there it is: a single brass screw holding the key machine to the counter, the one every other screw in the store is counting on. Lefty loosey. The wheel wobbles. The drawers shiver. The whole perfect store, built as one machine, can't decide what to hold, and it gently unfolds, spilling Crystal Street out onto the roundabout grass. You put the screw in Magda's open hand. She stares at it as if it's the first loose thing she's held in a year.
success.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume unscrewing a single brass screw at the base of a sparking key-cutting machine, a perfect hardware store unfolding like a puzzle box around them, neighbors spilling onto moonlit grass

failure.text: You find a screw that looks loose and pull it, and it's a decoy. "I put that one there for you," Magda says. "I learn." Every drawer in the store locks at once.
failure.art: A woman with a crown of brass screws behind a hardware counter holding up a single screw with a knowing look, rows of drawers slamming shut, a teenager in costume stepping back

choices.label: Throw your weight on the key machine's crank and run it backward, like the night you pried everything loose

success.text: That week she bolted everything down: the windows, the street, the Glitter Box's spotlight. Every time, you pried it loose with your own two hands. So you grab the key machine's big iron crank and throw your whole weight against it, the wrong way. Lefty loosey. The wheel screams and spins backward, and every screw in the store backs out a quarter-turn at once, then another, raining onto the floor. Chains slide off wrists. The aisles sag. Magda grabs the crank, and for one long second you are both straining against it. Then she lets go and steps back, staring at her hands, while the perfect store rattles apart around her into ten thousand loose screws on the roundabout grass.
success.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume heaving a big iron crank backward on a sparking key-cutting machine, screws raining from the walls, silver chains slipping off neighbors' wrists, a woman in an orange apron stepping back in shock

failure.text: The crank won't budge. She rests one hand on it, calmly, and turns it the right way. Righty tighty. A silver chain loops your wrist, soft as a watchband. You can still fight, just not like this.
failure.art: A woman with a crown of brass screws calmly turning a key-machine crank with one hand, a thin silver chain looping around a costumed teenager's wrist, sparks drifting across a perfect hardware store

choices.label: Tell her what you saw her holding on to the night before, then hold out your hand and ask to loosen one

success.text: "Last night I saw what you're holding on to," you tell her. "You kept every piece of him. You just never asked anyone to help you hold it." You lay the sign, the green ledger and his letter on the counter, open to FORGIVEN and to MAGDI. She reads her father's handwriting without touching it. You hold out your hand, palm up. "Can I loosen one?" For a long moment the key wheel is the only sound in the store. Then she nods, and you turn the first brass screw out of her crown, gently, lefty loosey. She takes the next one out herself. Then she walks the aisles beside you, asking every neighbor, "Do you want this off?", and waiting for each answer before she touches a single chain.
success.art: A woman behind a hardware counter letting brass screws fall from her gray-streaked hair, a teenager in costume holding out an open palm, an old green ledger and a weathered shop board on the counter, neighbors' chains loosening

failure.text: She looks at your open hand as if it's a trick. "Everyone who ever asked me anything wanted something," she says, and the chains in the aisles cinch tight. She still needs to hear it. Slow down.
failure.art: A woman with a crown of brass screws gripping a hardware counter, a teenager in costume holding out an open palm, silver chains tightening around neighbors' wrists in the aisles

choices.label: Throw the breaker and wreck the key machine

success.text: Sparks, a bang, darkness. The perfect store rattles apart into ten thousand loose screws that rain down onto the roundabout grass. Screwhead falls with them, and lands as just a woman in an orange apron, asleep on the lawn, remembering nothing at all.
success.art: A key-cutting machine exploding in sparks as a hardware store bursts apart into a rain of screws over a suburban roundabout, a woman in an apron collapsing asleep on the grass

failure.text: The machine won't stop. Chains loop around your wrists, soft and certain as a seatbelt. "There," she says gently, almost kindly, and she does not ask. "Now you're safe."
failure.art: Silver chains wrapping a struggling teenager's wrists in front of a sparking key machine, a tall woman with a crown of brass screws looking down at them with pity

choices.label: Swap the labels on one drawer and let her try to fix it

success.text: You swap the quarter-inch and the three-eighths. She can't stand it. She fixes it. You swap two more. The crew starts swapping every label in the store, and she spins in place trying to correct everything at once until the box can't hold its own disorder and pops open, spilling the whole street out onto the lawn.
success.art: A teen crew frantically swapping labels on hundreds of hardware drawers while a woman with brass screws in her hair spins in panic trying to fix them, the walls of the store cracking open to the night sky

failure.text: She sees you do it. "I was doing my father's inventory at twelve, kid." Every drawer in the store slams shut at once like a giant clapping its hands, and your fingers are caught in one of them.
failure.art: Hundreds of drawers slamming shut at once along an endless wall, a teenager's hand caught in one, a woman behind the counter shaking her head

choices.label: Show her the sign, the ledger and her father's letter, then ask before you loosen anything

success.text: You set the old sign on the counter, open the green ledger to FORGIVEN, and read Laszlo's letter out loud. Magda's hands stop on the wheel. "He forgave all of them," she says. "Even the ones who went to the mall." You hold out your hand, palm up, and ask: "Can I loosen one?" Nobody has asked her anything in a year. She stares at you, then nods. One screw comes out of her crown, then another, falling ringing to the floor. "A chain somebody chooses is a promise," she says slowly. "One you put on them is a cage." She takes off the orange apron and goes aisle to aisle, asking each neighbor, "Do you want this off?", and turning each chain a quarter-turn the other way when they say yes.
success.art: A tearful woman reading an old letter at a hardware counter as brass screws fall from her loosened hair like rain, an open green ledger and a hand-painted sign before her, a teenager holding out an open palm, freed neighbors rubbing their wrists

failure.text: She grips the counter until it creaks. "Words don't hold anything together." You have everything she needs to hear, but she's wound too tight to hear it yet, and the whole store groans like a ship.
failure.art: A woman with a crown of brass screws gripping a hardware counter with white knuckles, a teenager holding out a letter, the store walls straining and bending

best.title: Keys Cut While You Wait
best.text: On November first Magda goes to Pinecrest and loosens her father's headstone a single quarter-turn so it can lean like everybody else's. Then she goes home and eats dinner. By December there's a card table at the Heartstone roundabout every Saturday: SZABO & DAUGHTER FIX-IT, painted crooked on purpose. Toasters, tape players, bike chains, a quarter each, pay when you can, and she asks before she fixes anything, because some people like their things a little broken. She keeps a green ledger. She lets the crew rearrange her toolbox however they want and only twitches a little. On Friday nights she leaves the table to Frankie, borrows Wade's leather jacket and goes dancing at the Glitter Box with her hair down and every screw out. She teaches you to cut a key, and the first one you make opens nothing at all, and she says that's fine, she'll keep it anyway.
best.art: A woman in a brown shop coat with her gray-streaked hair loose around her shoulders smiles behind a folding repair table on a suburban roundabout beside a purple crystal rock, a crookedly painted wooden board propped above her, broken toasters, tape players and a bike chain on the table, a green ledger open at her elbow, a line of teenagers and neighbors waiting with broken gadgets, bright Saturday morning sun, medium wide shot

good.title: Everything in Its Place
good.text: The store dissolves, the chains fall away, and Crystal Street wakes up with its houses back where they belong, slightly crooked. Magda goes back to the HomeMax and her orange apron. Sometimes, driving past at three a.m., you see her alone in a lit aisle straightening a display that was already straight, and you wonder what it was she lost, and who she had to be to keep it.
good.art: A lone gaunt woman in an orange apron with brass screws pinned through her gray-streaked bun straightens an already perfect pyramid display in a brightly lit, empty big-box hardware store at three in the morning, seen through the glass front doors from a dark parking lot, a teenager in the passenger seat of a passing station wagon in the foreground, white store light and dark blue night, wide shot

bittersweet.title: A Quarter-Turn Too Tight
bittersweet.text: You survive the week and so does most of the street, but a few neighbors never quite loosen up. The Delgados mow their lawn in perfect stripes at six a.m. every day now and never laugh at the same jokes twice. Magda moves away in the spring without saying goodbye. On your wrist there's a faint white line where a chain once was, and on bad days it itches like a screw being turned.
bittersweet.art: A suburban front lawn at dawn mowed in perfect straight stripes, a stiff middle-aged couple standing on the porch side by side with identical fixed smiles, a teenager on the sidewalk in a jacket rubbing a thin pale line around their wrist, mist over the street, pale pink sunrise light, medium wide shot from the sidewalk

bad.title: Perfect Order
bad.text: You wake on November first and your life is perfectly organized. Your tapes are alphabetized. Your hair is combed. Every evening at six you stand at your mailbox with your hands folded and wait for nothing in particular. Nobody asked you, and you can't remember how to say stop. Your crew tries to make you laugh. You check your watch, and you smile, and you don't move at all.
bad.art: A teenager with neatly combed hair and a buttoned shirt stands perfectly still at a suburban mailbox at dusk with hands folded and a calm small smile, wristwatch showing six, three friends in bright Halloween costumes crowded around trying to make them laugh, one waving a rubber chicken, orange dusk light and long shadows, medium shot
